summary:
I've been chipping away at a Japanese-learning app I build for myself in spare time. The interesting problem this year wasn't content — it's that the practice conversations felt hollow even though there was plenty of vocabulary underneath. I measured it: for several of the characters you can talk to, running through their whole question menu, one answer covered 100% of the twelve questions. The variety was real, but predictable, so there was nothing left to actually listen for. The fix isn't more content, it's keying each character's opinions to the concept behind a question rather than the topic label, so the same character can plausibly say different things depending on what's actually being asked.

For BudgetTracker, I built a set of read-only tools that let my home AI assistant answer questions about spending directly against the database — eleven of them, covering things like cash-flow projections and account integrity checks. The tools do their math in SQL rather than handing raw rows to the model, so a question like "what's my run rate" gets a deterministic number instead of an LLM doing arithmetic. Account access is scoped per API key, so the assistant can only ever see the accounts it's explicitly been given.

On the infrastructure side, I run Switchboard, a small proxy that arbitrates a single GPU across half a dozen things that all want it — a chat model, an image generator, a couple of specialized inference backends. Only one really fits in memory at a time, so the proxy evicts whoever's loaded, waits for the card to actually free up, then loads whatever's needed next. The part I had to get right was making a cold reload cheap: the chat model now saves its attention cache to disk right before it gets evicted and restores it on the way back in, so a model swap costs seconds instead of re-processing tens of thousands of tokens of context from scratch.

I also spent a day chasing an audio bug in a D&D campaign app I use with friends — a whole session where nobody could hear anyone over video. The room connected fine, everyone saw each other's camera feed, but the code that pulled in video tracks never had a matching line for audio; a WebRTC audio track only makes sound once it's attached to a media element, and nothing attached it. Wrote a small two-browser test harness — real app code, fake devices, no manual clicking — to prove the fix actually delivers sound end to end before trusting it.

highlights.oneLiner: Found character replies were predictable from the question; keying opinions to concept not topic label.
Built 11 read-only MCP tools so the home assistant answers spending questions with SQL-computed, scoped numbers.
GPU arbiter for a shared card; added KV-cache save/restore so model swaps cost seconds, not a re-prefill.
